title: Die Last der Nachfolge: Roms Zukunft sichern
excerpt: Ich habe keine Söhne. Dies verfolgt mich mehr als ich zugebe. Wie stellt man sicher, dass das System, das man aufgebaut hat, den eigenen Tod überlebt?
author: augustus

content.diary:
I am seventy years old—an age few men reach, fewer still reach with their power intact. Yet increasingly, I find myself thinking about the question that would have seemed arrogant to contemplate in my youth: what happens after I am gone?

I have built something remarkable here in Rome. The civil wars are ended, commerce flourishes, the empire is secure. But all of this rests, to a significant degree, on the structures I have created and the relationships I maintain. When I am gone, will it endure? Or will ambitious men tear apart what I have built, using the army and the Senate as tools for factional warfare, just as occurred before?

The problem of succession has been before me for years. Nature itself has been frustrating; my many hopes for male heirs have come to nothing. My only daughter, Julia, has given me no grandsons who survive. I have adopted several potential heirs—Marcellus, Agrippa, now the young Tiberius—but adoption is not the same as blood succession. Each time I have thought I had settled the succession, death has intervened.

I have tried to solve this through institutional means. I have ensured that the Senate understands the succession should pass to whoever I have officially adopted. I have made certain that my closest associates know my wishes. The Praetorian Guard is personally loyal to me; I hope they will transfer that loyalty to my chosen heir. But will these measures prove sufficient?

There is no perfect solution. I could declare a military monarchy outright, abandon all pretense of republican form, and establish a clear line of succession based on my bloodline or my explicit designation. But that would generate resistance, resentment, plots against whatever heir I name. The system I have created depends partly on the appearance of republican continuity; if I shatter that appearance, the new emperor will face opposition from senators who believe the traditional order should be restored.

Alternatively, I could weaken my system deliberately, creating checks and balances that prevent any individual from accumulating the absolute power I possess. But that risks inviting factional conflict to resume.

My best hope is this: that the system itself—the arrangement of institutions, the distribution of power, the alignment of interests I have created—is robust enough to survive transition to a new emperor. The legions remain loyal to Rome and her institutions, not to my person alone. The Senate, though diminished compared to the Republic, retains enough importance that ambitious men will seek its favor. The commercial classes have prospered under my system and will resist chaos that threatens their prosperity.

I have also worked to ensure that whoever succeeds me has been groomed for the position. Tiberius has served as military commander, has experience in the provinces, has learned how to balance military power with political legitimacy. Perhaps he will prove adequate.

But I am under no illusions. History shows that succession is the moment of greatest danger for any regime. I have made my decisions; I have put structures in place. Now I must accept that I cannot control the future as I have controlled the present. There is a certain humility required in accepting the limits of even the greatest leader's power.

I think sometimes about what I will leave behind. The Res Gestae Divi Augusti—the record of my accomplishments that I have prepared for display throughout the empire. Future Romans will read of how I ended the civil wars, expanded the frontiers, brought peace and prosperity. That record will matter more than my name or memory. Rome, I believe, will endure. The specific form it takes after my death—that remains beyond my control.
content.scientific:
Augustus faced what is termed the 'succession problem'—the challenge of ensuring that the political system he created would survive his death and transition smoothly to a successor. This problem was particularly acute because Augustus held no formally absolute position; his power derived from a combination of military resources, political skill, and the general acceptance that he served Rome's interests. Upon his death, would this combination of factors transfer to an heir, or would the system collapse into renewed factional conflict?

Augustus never produced a male heir capable of surviving to adulthood. His only child, Julia, produced children by her husbands, but the grandsons either died in childhood or, in the case of Gaius and Lucius Caesar, died in late adolescence or early adulthood before they could be established as their grandfather's successor.

In response to this biological reality, Augustus developed a succession strategy based on adoption. He adopted promising political and military figures who appeared capable of managing the Principate. The sequence of adoptions changed multiple times: Marcellus (his nephew, son-in-law, and adopted heir) died in 23 BCE; Marcus Agrippa served as co-ruler and likely intended successor until his death in 12 BCE; Julia's sons Gaius and Lucius Caesar were adopted and groomed but both died; ultimately Tiberius, the son of Augustus's wife Livia from her first marriage, became the designated heir.

Augustus's approach to succession involved several components. First, he published records of his intentions, most significantly through the Res Gestae Divi Augusti (The Deeds of Divine Augustus), an inscription describing his accomplishments and intended to establish his legacy. This text also implicitly defined what succession meant: continuation of the system of organized peace and Republican form that Augustus had established.

Second, Augustus worked to integrate his intended heir into the power structure gradually. Before being adopted, Tiberius held significant military commands, served as consul, and managed substantial provinces. This process of integration gave the heir both practical experience and established him as a legitimate political figure in his own right, not merely the emperor's choice.

Third, Augustus maintained that succession was not about personal inheritance of property or dynasty, but about transfer of the offices and relationships that gave him power. The Senate would ratify the succession; the Praetorian Guard would transfer loyalty; the legions would recognize the new emperor. This framing emphasized institutional continuity rather than dynastic succession, though in practice the result was similar.

Fourth, Augustus attempted to surround the succession with the appearance of choice, consensus, and republican legitimacy. He portrayed his successor not as a king-to-be imposed by military force, but as the choice of the Senate and the will of the people. Whether this reflected reality or was a carefully constructed fiction remains debated among historians; regardless, maintaining the fiction of republican legitimacy was important for political stability.

Historically, Augustus's succession strategy proved partially successful and partially vulnerable. Tiberius did become emperor after Augustus's death in 14 CE, and he was generally accepted by the Senate, the Praetorian Guard, and the legions. The transition avoided the civil war that might have occurred if multiple factions had presented rival candidates.

However, Tiberius was widely unpopular, widely believed to have been a reluctant heir forced upon Rome by Augustus's lack of alternatives. This unpopularity contributed to political instability and suspicion during his reign. Moreover, the succession strategy created a precedent that subsequent emperors attempted to follow, often with varying degrees of success.

The succession problem illuminates a fundamental tension in Augustus's system: he had created what appeared to be a Republic but functioned as an autocracy. In a true Republic, succession would involve competitive elections; in a true autocracy, succession would be determined by dynastic succession laws or other clear mechanisms. Augustus's system was vulnerable at precisely the point where the facade of republicanism had to confront the reality of autocratic succession.
